title: Flight 1549: Both Engines Lost Thrust at 2,818 Feet — What the NTSB Found (Hudson River, 2009)
description:
January 15, 2009: US Airways flight 1549, an Airbus A320, loses almost all thrust in both engines after hitting a flock of Canada geese 2,818 feet above the ground, about two minutes after takeoff from LaGuardia. Three and a half minutes later it is on the Hudson River. All 155 people on board survived. Explained second by second, only with the NTSB final report NTSB/AAR-10/03 and the investigation's public docket: flight data, cockpit voice recorder, radar track, simulator tests and the board's findings.

The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the ingestion of large birds into each engine, which resulted in an almost total loss of thrust in both engines and the subsequent ditching on the Hudson River. Contributing to the fuselage damage and resulting unavailability of the aft slide/rafts were the FAA's approval of ditching certification without determining whether pilots could attain the ditching parameters without engine thrust, the lack of industry flight crew training and guidance on ditching techniques, and the captain's resulting difficulty maintaining his intended airspeed on final approach due to the task saturation resulting from the emergency situation. The NTSB also listed four factors that contributed to survivability.

firstComment: The NTSB's simulator pilots made it back to a runway in 8 of 15 runs with an immediate turn — and 0 of 1 after a 35-second delay. What do you think: how much time does a crew really need to understand that thrust is not coming back?
